newsitem.title: USA: Texas-New Mexico Power to open markets.
newsitem.headline: Texas-New Mexico Power to open markets.

text.p: Texas-New Mexico Power Co on Thursday filed tentative plans with Texas regulators to open its electric markets in the state to competition beginning next year, officials said.

The utility, a unit of Fort Worth-based TNP Enterprises Inc, proposed a five-year transition to retail competition beginning on Jan. 1, 1998 in its patchwork service territory covering parts of north, central and southeast Texas.

The plan would cut residential rates by two percent on January 1, 1998, 2000 and 2002, and cut commercial rates by one percent on each of those dates. Industrial rates would be frozen during the transition, the company said.
By shifting depreciation, capping its return on equity, and taking accelerated and normal depreciation, the company would recover an estimated $210.5 million in stranded costs, a spokesman said.

Remaining stranded costs, estimated at $60 million to $62 million, would be "trued-up" at fair market value at the end of the transition period and collected through a charge on electric transmission and distribution, the spokesman said.
Texas-New Mexico Power withdrew an earlier plan to open its Texas markets while state legislators debated a deregulation bill that eventually was defeated in this year's biennial session.
"(Deregulation) is going to happen with or without us, so we ought to be proactive," spokeswoman Valerie Smith said of the company's decision to refile the plan.
TNP's proposal was expected to find support at the Texas Public Utility Commission, which has been balking at a rival seven-year transition plan submitted by Entergy.

"(PUC) Chairman Pat Wood pointed to this TNP filing as having many of the components of the model for future rate settlements in Texas for the next two year," HSBC James Capel analyst Daniel Ford said earlier this week.

Texas-New Mexico Power has begun a pilot program in New Mexico allowing about 60 residential and business customers to choose their energy provider, a first step in opening that market to competition.
